answer: The BLIS 6-knob configuration space (1800 configs, 4 objectives) has a hierarchically structured Pareto front dominated by GPU count (tp*instances), which creates discrete throughput tiers. Within each tier, the Pareto front's complexity lives in the 'partial preemption' zone: specific (kv_blocks, max_num_running_reqs, scheduler) combinations at low-instance tiers (ni=1, ni=2) where cache pressure causes preemptions that differentiate configs by ttft_p99. Above the preemption threshold (~4500-5000 blocks), additional kv_blocks have zero effect; below it, TTFT p99 spikes 100-250x. block_size=32 is strictly Pareto-dominant (halves kv_blocks for same cache capacity). The effective dimensionality is ~3 (GPU count, KV sufficiency, concurrency sufficiency). The Pareto front has only 23-43 distinct metric tuples (depending on rate and seed) out of 1800 configs. A structure-aware search (v4) with 3 phases — deterministic tier sampling, diversity-directed expansion of rich tiers, and neighbor expansion — finds 100% of Pareto tuples at rates 50-200 across 3 seeds using only 200 evaluations (11% of space), in ~16-44 seconds. The algorithm generalizes to a different model (llama-2-7b: 97.1% recall). Pareto tuple count is seed-stable at high rates (rate=100: 35-39 tuples, 1.11x range) but seed-sensitive at low rates (rate=50: 23-38 tuples, 1.65x range).
